newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises on news of European stability pact.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises on news of European stability pact.

text.p: The dollar rose Friday, bolstered by a landmark European pact on budget discipline and a later-denied rumour that Japanese officials desired a stronger dollar against the yen, dealers said.
The German mark weakened against the dollar and most other European currencies after a hard-fought Franco-German battle over fiscal discipline standards ended with a signed pact.
The pact takes the 15-nation bloc a major step closer to the goal of a single European currency in 1999.

"The pact is bullish for the dollar with the implication being that Europe is a little closer to agreement on European monetary union, which is basically deutschemark negative," said Steven Walker, senior trader at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in New York.
"If it's deutschemark negative, it's got to be dollar positive," he added.

The dollar posted early U.S. gains against the yen on market rumours that a Washington-based consultancy had issued a report saying that Japanese officials would tolerate an exchange rate as high as 120 yen per dollar. The consultancy later officially denied it had put out any such report, which eased the dollar's strength.
The dollar closed at 113.90 yen per dollar, up from 113.17.
New of the European pact also helped limit the dollar's gains against the yen, because it encouraged traders to sell the mark, not only against the dollar, but against the yen as well.

Other factors strengthening the dollar were talk that a U.S. money fund made a large purchase of dollars for yen, possibly as much as $1 billion, and strong buying by Japanese trust banks, eager to own dollars ahead of their expected participation in next week's auction of two- and five-year U.S. Treasury notes.
The dollar closed higher at 1.5545 marks compared with Thursday's close of 1.5410 marks.

The dollar remained somewhat captive to a gyrating stock market for a third straight session, with dollar ups and downs roughly matching the swings in the Dow Jones industrials. The Dow traded sharply lower, then surged back to end almost unchanged.
"The fact that the stock market is ending rather neutral is helping the dollar. When it was off earlier today, the dollar was pressing its lows against European currencies," Ullrich said.
The dollar has been dragged lower over the past two trading days by heavy losses in U.S. stock markets.
The dollar recovered from an early selloff against the Swiss franc that occurred after Swiss National Bank member Bruno Gehrig said the Swiss franc was no longer clearly overvalued.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.3250 Swiss francs compared with 1.3110 francs and to Canadian $1.3629 from C$1.3587. Sterling fell slightly to $1.6565 from $1.6570.
